item.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=failure+modes+of+instruction-following+in+AI+systems+when+human+objectives+are+contextually+inadequate&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7433399\", \"title\": [\"When Agentic AI Breaks Software Quality Assurance: Failure Modes, Reliability Risks, and Governance Strategies for Autonomous Testing Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The emergence of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is changing software quality assurance from a predominantly human-directed activity into an increasingly autonomous process in which AI systems can generate tests, execute programs, interpret failures, modify test suites, and iteratively refine their actions. While these capabilities promise substantial improvements in testing speed, coverage, and engineering productivity, they also introduce a distinct class of quality risks. An autonomous testing agent can produce a technically executable test that encodes an incorrect assumption, misinterpret a failure, optimize for coverage rather than meaningful defect detection, or repeatedly reinforce an erroneous testing strategy. This article examines these risks through an integrative review of research on large language models (LLMs), automated software testing, AI-assisted software engineering, and AI governance. The analysis identifies six interconnected failure modes: erroneous test generation, defective test oracles, autonomous error propagation, coverage-driven quality illusion, contextual and repository misunderstanding, and governance and accountability failure. The article argues that the central challenge is not simply whether AI can generate valid tests, but whether autonomous testing systems can maintain trustworthy quality judgments under uncertainty. Drawing on empirical evidence from recent studies of ChatGPT, LLM-based test generation, TestGen-LLM, and software-engineering agents, the article proposes a risk-based governance model built around bounded autonomy, independent verification, traceability, human checkpoints, continuous monitoring, and explicit escalation mechanisms.
